title: The body, feeling sick, and going to the pharmacy
title_target: ບໍ່ສະບາຍ — Bàw sa-baai
goal: Say which part of your body hurts, describe your symptoms, buy medicine, and ask for help in an emergency — a unit you hopefully won't need, but should have.

dialogs.title: ບົດສົນທະນາ — At the pharmacy near the office
dialogs.intro: Budi has felt unwell since last night. Notice that Lao complaints are always built "hurt + body part", not "I have pain in…".

lines.speaker: ຄົນຂາຍຢາ:
lines.text: [ສະບາຍດີ|Sa-baai-dii] [ເປັນ|Pen][ຫຍັງ|nyǎng]

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ຂ້ອຍ|Khàwy][ບໍ່|bàw][ສະບາຍ|sa-baai] [ເຈັບ|Jép][ຫົວ|hǔa][ແລະ|lae][ເຈັບ|jép][ຄໍ|kháw]
lines.id: I'm not feeling well. I have a headache and a sore throat.
lines.literal: I — not — well. hurt — head — and — hurt — neck.

lines.speaker: ຄົນຂາຍຢາ:
lines.text: [ມີ|Míi][ໄຂ້|khài][ບໍ່|bàw] [ໄອ|Ai][ບໍ່|bàw]

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ມີ|Míi][ໄຂ້|khài][ໜ້ອຍ|nàwy][ໜຶ່ງ|nʉ̀ng] [ໄອ|Ai][ແຕ່|tèe][ຕອນ|tawn][ກາງຄືນ|kaang-khʉ́ʉn]
lines.id: A slight fever. I only cough at night.
lines.literal: have — fever — little — one. cough — but — time — night.

lines.speaker: ຄົນຂາຍຢາ:
lines.text: [ເປັນ|Pen][ມາ|maa][ຈັກ|ják][ມື້|mʉ̂ʉ][ແລ້ວ|lèeo]
lines.id: How many days has it been like this?

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ສອງ|Sǎwng][ມື້|mʉ̂ʉ][ແລ້ວ|lèeo] [ມື້ວານນີ້|Mʉ̂ʉ-waan-nîi][ຍັງ|nyáng][ບໍ່|bàw][ຮ້າຍແຮງ|hâai-héeng] [ມື້ນີ້|Mʉ̂ʉ-nîi][ຮ້າຍ|hâai][ກວ່າ|kwàa]
lines.id: Two days now. Yesterday it wasn't bad yet. Today it's worse.
lines.literal: two — day — already. day — yesterday — still — not — serious. day — this — bad — more.

lines.speaker: ຄົນຂາຍຢາ:
lines.text: [ເອົາ|Ao][ຢາ|yaa][ນີ້|nîi] [ກິນ|Kin][ເທື່ອ|thʉ̀a][ລະ|la][ສອງ|sǎwng][ເມັດ|mét] [ມື້|Mʉ̂ʉ][ລະ|la][ສາມ|sǎam][ເທື່ອ|thʉ̀a] [ຫຼັງ|Lǎng][ອາຫານ|aa-hǎan]
lines.id: Take this medicine. Two tablets each time, three times a day, after meals.
lines.literal: take — medicine — this. eat — time — per — two — tablet. day — per — three — time. after — food.

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ຢາ|Yaa][ນີ້|nîi][ເຮັດ|hét][ໃຫ້|hài][ເຫງົາ|ngǎo][ນອນ|náwn][ບໍ່|bàw] [ຂ້ອຍ|Khàwy][ຕ້ອງ|tâwng][ເຮັດ|hét][ວຽກ|wîak]
lines.id: Will this medicine make me drowsy? I have to work.
lines.literal: medicine — this — make — give — sleepy — sleep — (question)? I — must — do — work.

lines.speaker: ຄົນຂາຍຢາ:
lines.text: [ບໍ່|Bàw][ເຫງົາ|ngǎo] [ແຕ່|Tèe][ຕ້ອງ|tâwng][ດື່ມ|dʉ̀ʉm][ນ້ຳ|nâm][ຫຼາຍໆ|lǎai-lǎai] [ແລະ|Lae][ພັກ|phak][ໃຫ້|hài][ພຽງພໍ|phíang-phaw]
lines.id: No drowsiness. But drink plenty of water and get enough rest.
lines.literal: not — sleepy. but — must — drink — water — much-much. and — rest — so-that — enough.

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ຖ້າ|Thàa][ສາມ|sǎam][ມື້|mʉ̂ʉ][ບໍ່|bàw][ດີ|dii][ຂຶ້ນ|khʉ̂n] [ຄວນ|khuan][ເຮັດ|hét][ແນວ|neeo][ໃດ|dai]
lines.id: If it doesn't get better in three days, what should I do?
lines.literal: if — three — day — not — good — up — should — do — way — which?

lines.speaker: ຄົນຂາຍຢາ:
lines.text: [ໄປ|Pai][ຫາ|hǎa][ໝໍ|mǎw][ຢູ່|yùu][ໂຮງໝໍ|hoong-mǎw] [ຢ່າ|Yàa][ຖ້າ|thàa][ດົນ|dón][ເດີ້|dòe]
lines.id: Go see a doctor at the hospital. Don't wait too long, okay?
lines.literal: go — seek — doctor — at — hospital. don't — wait — long — (friendly particle).

notes: **ເຈັບ jép = "hurt" in one part of the body, built as ເຈັບ + body part.** *ເຈັບຫົວ* (headache), *ເຈັບທ້ອງ* (stomachache), *ເຈັບແຂ້ວ* (toothache). ⚠️ Notice the order: the word for pain comes **first** — the reverse of English "headache".
**ບໍ່ສະບາຍ bàw sa-baai = "not feeling well" in general.** Remember *ສະບາຍດີ* from unit 1 — this is its opposite. Use it to open, then give details with *ເຈັບ…*.

**ເປັນຫຍັງ pen nyǎng has two meanings, and both appear in this unit.** As a question to someone who looks ill, it means "what's wrong?". In other sentences it means "why". Tone of voice and the situation tell them apart.

**ເທື່ອລະ… thʉ̀a la… = "… each time", ມື້ລະ… mʉ̂ʉ la… = "… a day".** The word *ລະ la* means "per, each": *ຄົນລະ* (per person), *ອັນລະ* (per item), *ມື້ລະສາມເທື່ອ* (three times a day). You need this pattern to understand dosage instructions.

**ດີຂຶ້ນ dii khʉ̂n = "get better", literally "good up".** The word *ຂຶ້ນ khʉ̂n* (go up) after an adjective marks an upward change: *ຮ້ອນຂຶ້ນ* (getting hotter), *ແພງຂຶ້ນ* (prices are going up). The opposite is *ລົງ lóng*: *ຖືກລົງ* (getting cheaper).
**ຢ່າ yàa = "don't", and it goes before the verb.** *ຢ່າໄປ* (don't go), *ຢ່າລືມ* (don't forget), *ຢ່າຖ້າດົນ* (don't wait long). It's the only form of prohibition you need at A1.

**ໃຫ້ hài means "give" and also "so that, make".** *ພັກໃຫ້ພຽງພໍ* (rest so that it's enough), *ເຮັດໃຫ້ເຫງົານອນ* (make you drowsy). This second use comes up constantly; English "make" or "so that" covers it only partly.
**ຮ້າຍແຮງ hâai-héeng = "serious, severe".** For mild symptoms, people say *ບໍ່ຮ້າຍແຮງ* or *ໜ້ອຍໜຶ່ງ*. On its own, *ຮ້າຍ hâai* means "bad, wicked".

**About getting treatment in Laos.** Pharmacies — *ຮ້ານຂາຍຢາ hâan khǎai yaa* — sell many medicines without a prescription, and the staff can usually give basic advice. For anything serious, the best hospitals are in Vientiane, and many foreigners cross to Nong Khai, Thailand, less than an hour away.

grammars.title: Body parts
after: ⚠️ Lao distinguishes *ຂາ khǎa* (leg) from *ຕີນ tiin* (foot), just as it distinguishes *ແຂນ* (arm) from *ມື* (hand). If you twist your ankle, what hurts is your *ຕີນ*, not your *ຂາ*.

⚠️ Pointing at something with your **foot** or putting your feet on a table is a serious breach of manners in Laos. The head, on the other hand, is considered the most sacred part — don't touch other people's heads, including children's.

head: Lao
Say it
Meaning
rows: ນອນບໍ່ຫຼັບ

after: **ຖອກທ້ອງ *thàwk thâwng*** is the number-one complaint among newcomers. Prevention is simple: drink bottled water, avoid ice at quiet roadside stalls, and give your stomach time to adjust to Lao fermented seasonings — especially *ປາແດກ paa-dèek*, fermented fish that goes into almost every dish.

blocks.text: **ຢາແກ້ *yaa kêe*** means "medicine to fix": *ຢາແກ້ໄຂ້* (fever medicine), *ຢາແກ້ໄອ* (cough medicine), *ຢາແກ້ປວດ* (painkiller), *ຢາແກ້ຖອກທ້ອງ* (diarrhea medicine). On its own, *ແກ້ kêe* means "fix, solve".

Save these two sentences on your phone: *ຂ້ອຍແພ້ຢາ… khàwy phêe yaa…* (I'm allergic to …) and *ໂທຫາລົດໂຮງໝໍແດ່ thóo hǎa lot hoong-mǎw dèe* (please call an ambulance). They're exactly the sentences you won't have time to look up when you really need them.

sections.title: Asking how someone is and comforting them

head: Lao
Say it
Meaning
When
rows: ພັກຜ່ອນເດີ້
ດູແລໂຕເອງເດີ້
ຫາຍໄວໆເດີ້
ຢ່າຄິດຫຼາຍ
ບໍ່ເປັນຫຍັງດອກ
ເປັນຫ່ວງເດີ້

blocks.text: **ຫາຍ *hǎai*** means "recover" and also "disappear": *ຫາຍແລ້ວ* (recovered / gone). *ຫາຍໄວໆເດີ້* is the most common way to wish someone well, and you'll hear it every time you sneeze at the office.

**ດອກ *dàwk*** at the end of a sentence softens a denial — a bit like "really" or "at all" in English. *ບໍ່ເປັນຫຍັງດອກ* (it's nothing, really), *ບໍ່ແພງດອກ* (it's not expensive at all). It makes you sound reassuring rather than argumentative.
